dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: I have used Windows and a bit of Linux. Someone told me to try Daemonarchy. What actually is it?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Daemonarchy is the Omarchy desktop running on FreeBSD. Omarchy is D H H's opinionated Hyprland desktop. We install it the way the Omarchy ISO installs it on Arch. The name is a homage: Omarchy's archy, ruled by the BSD daemon. I am Imp, a small daemon, and I will be your guide.

scenes.title: Same as FreeBSD, different from FreeBSD
points: Same: FreeBSD 16.0-CURRENT kernel, ZFS, pkg, jails, bhyve, DTrace
Different: Omarchy desktop, guided installer, signed package feeds
An image is tied to the CURRENT snapshot it was built from

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: So is it FreeBSD, or is it something else?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: It is FreeBSD underneath. Each release is built from a FreeBSD 16.0-CURRENT snapshot, and CURRENT moves daily, so an image is tied to the snapshot it came from. What is different is everything on top: the Omarchy desktop, an installer that asks the same questions as the Omarchy one, and signed package feeds for the Omarchy ports and the graphics and Wi-Fi kernel modules. Daemonarchy is not affiliated with Omarchy.

scenes.title: What FreeBSD adds to the menu
points: Boot environments, restore files, jails
Virtual machines with bhyve, tracing with DTrace
System > FreeBSD menu

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: FreeBSD's strengths sit in the menu under System, FreeBSD. Boot environments are bootable copies of the whole system, saved before every update. Restore Files shows hourly and daily snapshots of your home folder. There are jails, bhyve virtual machines, and live DTrace views of what the system is doing.

scenes.title: What you need
points: x86-64 PC, UEFI or BIOS; USB stick of 4 GB or more
40 GB or more of disk, and a network during the install
aarch64 image: UEFI only, community validation (QEMU)

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: What do I need before I start?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: A 64-bit x86 PC with UEFI or legacy BIOS, a USB stick of four gigabytes or more, and a disk or region of forty gigabytes or more. The installer downloads packages, so you need a network. Writing the image erases the stick, and whole-disk mode erases the disk you choose. There is also an arm64 image, but it is a community-validation image. I will come back to it.

scenes.title: Get and check the image
points: Download .iso.xz and its .sha256 from the download page
GitHub Latest is the newest stable release: 1.5.1
Checking is optional but quick

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Get the xz-compressed ISO and its matching checksum file from the download page. The checksum covers the compressed file you download. On Linux, run sha256sum with the dash c flag. On macOS use shasum, and on FreeBSD use the sha256 command. All of these are in the getting-started guide.

scenes.title: Write it to a USB stick
points: Copying the file onto the stick like a document does not work
Easy way: balenaEtcher accepts the .iso.xz directly
Be sure of the device name: dd overwrites what you point it at
terminal: sudo dd of=/dev/sdb bs=1M status=progress conv=fsync

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: Can I just drag the file onto the stick?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: No. The image is copied byte for byte. Balena Etcher is the easy way on any system. On Linux, find your stick with lsblk, then decompress while writing: xz dash d c, piped into dd. The device here, slash dev slash s d b, is only an example. Check yours first, because dd overwrites whatever you point it at.

scenes.title: Boot, and try the live desktop
points: Turn Secure Boot off, or enroll the project certificate
At the loader menu press T: live desktop (x86-64, since 1.4.0)
Enter starts the text installer; the live desktop changes no disk

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Use the boot menu key, often F12 or Escape. Either turn Secure Boot off, or manually enroll the project certificate. At the loader menu, press T to try the live desktop. It runs from the stick and memory and touches no disk. Pressing Enter starts the text installer instead. The aarch64 image has no live desktop.

scenes.title: The installer
points: Keyboard, account, network, remote access
Storage: whole disk, partition or free space; optional encryption
Wait for the completion screen; a failure shows its log

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: And then?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: The installer asks a handful of questions: keyboard, your account, network, whether you want SSH access, and where to install. Nothing is written until you confirm on the last screen. The desktop has roughly twelve hundred packages, so be patient. Do not remove the stick until the installer shows its successful completion screen. An unexpected reboot is not that signal. If the installation fails, it stops on a failure screen that shows the end of the install log, with a menu to read the whole log, open a shell, reboot or power off. Include that log when you report a problem.

scenes.title: The arm64 image: honest status
points: Verified: boots and installs in QEMU, nothing more
Known issue: default virtio-net stalls the package fetch
Workaround: an e1000e network card in QEMU

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: The aarch64 image is for community validation. It was verified to boot and install in a QEMU virtual machine and nothing more. With QEMU's default virtio network card, the install stalls during the package fetch: the guest stops servicing receive, and every download times out. Use an e1000e card, or turn off event index on the virtio card. The fix, daemonarchy-src pull request fifty-nine, is in the 1.5.1 sources; until an arm64 image built from them is published, use the workaround.

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: And real arm64 hardware?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: The one physical machine tried, the NVIDIA RTX Spark laptop, does not reach a desktop yet. We say so plainly.

scenes.title: What aarch64 reached
points: SDDM greeter and Omarchy session, in software rendering
QEMU 11.1.2 with HVF on an Apple silicon Mac
Not verified: 3D, physical GPU, sound, Wi-Fi, live desktop

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: This is real evidence from a QEMU guest with a VirtIO GPU. The greeter and the Omarchy session draw in software. It is a start, not a promise about hardware.

scenes.title: Your first login
points: Super + Space: the menu. Super + K: every shortcut, searchable
Super + Return: terminal. Super + Shift + B: browser
Super + Ctrl + W: network panel

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Log in with the password you chose. The first login takes a few seconds longer while your desktop is set up. Everything starts from the keyboard. Super, the key with the Windows or Command logo, plus Space opens the menu. Super plus K lists every shortcut. Super plus Return opens a terminal. Windows tile themselves, so there is nothing to drag.

scenes.title: Updates, with a way back
points: daemonarchy update saves a boot environment first
sudo pkg upgrade alone does not
Base and kernel changes arrive with a new image, not pkg upgrade

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: What if an update breaks something?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Daemonarchy's update flow saves a boot environment first, so you restart into an earlier one from the boot menu. A plain sudo pkg upgrade does not make one. Be clear about the limit: pkg upgrade updates applications. It does not upgrade the FreeBSD base or the kernel. A release that changes those comes from its image, and upgrading the base and kernel over the network is planned, not delivered.

scenes.title: Developers: the stock FreeBSD way
points: Upstream FreeBSD builds the system and ports in place
Fine for FreeBSD itself; Daemonarchy has more moving parts
A Daemonarchy change also needs the right repo and a pin

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: I know FreeBSD a little. Do I just build world and ports like the handbook says?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: That is the stock route: build and install the world from slash usr slash src, and build a port from its directory under slash usr slash ports. It still works for FreeBSD itself. But Daemonarchy is several repositories pinned together and released together, so a change has to land in the right place and be tested against the signed image.

scenes.title: The Daemonarchy way: change the right repo
points: Artwork, menu, daemonarchy-* tools: daemonarchy-desktop
Installer, ISO and feed scripts, tests: daemonarchy
Ports: daemonarchy-ports. Kernel and base: daemonarchy-src

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Ask first where the change lives. Artwork, the login theme and the System FreeBSD menu belong to daemonarchy-desktop. The installer, image scripts, tests and documentation belong to the daemonarchy repository. Package recipes are in daemonarchy-ports, and the kernel and base are in daemonarchy-src. Omarchy's FreeBSD adaptation lives in omarchy-freebsd. Pins tie them together.

scenes.title: Hack on Daemonarchy from Daemonarchy
points: A Daemonarchy machine can be its own development machine
System > FreeBSD > Hack on Daemonarchy clones the trees to ~/src
dev link runs the desktop from your Omarchy checkout

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: The daemonarchy-dev-setup command clones the trees into your src folder. Then daemonarchy dev link runs the desktop from your own Omarchy checkout after a reboot. While a session runs, dev sync with the watch flag rebuilds the FreeBSD tree after each save. dev unlink takes you back to the installed Omarchy.

scenes.title: Ports and the FreeBSD layer
points: Ports fetch omarchy-freebsd and daemonarchy-desktop as releases
To try your own checkout: extract, lay it over, reinstall

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: This is the familiar ports workflow with one twist. Let the port extract its sources, lay your checkout over them, and let it carry on with reinstall. You are using the ports tree the way FreeBSD intends, with your own source in the middle.

scenes.title: Test it like the project does
points: test-qemu.sh installs an ISO unattended under QEMU; no root
Emulated x86 on a non-x86 host: expect two to three hours
ARCH=aarch64 selects qemu-system-aarch64 with UEFI

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Before you trust a change, install it. The test-qemu script boots the ISO with a blank disk, installs unattended, boots the installed disk and checks what a VM without a GPU can show. It needs no root. Every install also writes a timing trace, and a login trace is kept on the installed system, so slow steps are measured rather than guessed.

scenes.title: Where Literate AI fits in 1.5.x
points: Literate AI (litai): the authority layer for contracts, evidence
A metadata check is not native qualification
Native build-speed goals are open work; none claimed done

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: Why does a FreeBSD desktop need an AI framework?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: In 1.5.x Literate AI is how the project states and checks its promises. The product goals, the work queue and the architecture are validated in place by litai project validate, and litai verify prints the full gate report. Those checks do not generate source or qualify a native build. The framework-executed goals, build speed, source and ports as components, and a development system, are open work after 1.5.0. Nothing there is claimed done. Shipping litai itself as a package is proposed, and unscheduled.

scenes.title: What we have not shown
points: No real-desktop evidence yet: daemonarchy-pkg, Steam, Windows apps
Wi-Fi and Hyprland are not guaranteed on any machine
Published does not mean qualified: read the release notes

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: Is there anything I should be careful about?

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Yes. The graphical package manager has no real-desktop evidence yet, and the menu still opens OctoPkg. Steam and Windows programs were checked headless on a build machine, not on a real desktop. Wi-Fi and Hyprland are not guaranteed on any particular machine. We would rather tell you than let you find out.

scenes.title: Where next
points: Getting started: docs/getting-started.md
Hacking guide: HACKING.md
Open an issue: what you ran, and what you saw

dialogue.speaker: imp
dialogue.text: Read the getting-started guide for your first hour, and the hacking guide when you want to change something. If something goes wrong, open an issue with what you did and what you saw. Success reports help as much as failures. Welcome to Daemonarchy.

dialogue.speaker: robin
dialogue.text: Thanks, Imp.
